title: The Guru's script
hook: at Khadur, Guru Angad shapes and teaches the Gurmukhi letters so ordinary people can read the hymns

segments.voice: Yesterday, ang: a limb, and the name Angad, part of my own body. Your line was passing the light. What did you teach someone who could carry it on? Day forty-five.

Think about the first time you read something by yourself. A cereal box, a street sign, a picture book. Something clicked, and a whole world that had belonged to grown-ups suddenly belonged to you too. For most people in the Punjab of the 1500s, that click never came. Reading was for priests, scholars and clerks. Sacred texts were in Sanskrit or Arabic or Persian, languages ordinary farmers didn't speak, and in scripts they couldn't read. And Guru Nanak's hymns, sung in the people's own language, were being passed along by memory and in rough notes. The new Guru, Angad, moved to a village called Khadur, and there, tradition says, he sat down with the children. Today, the letters he taught.
screen: `THE FIRST TIME YOU READ ALONE.` → `READING WAS FOR THE FEW.` → `GURU ANGAD SITS WITH THE CHILDREN.`

segments.voice: The script is called Gurmukhi. Guru is the teacher, and mukh is the mouth, so Gurmukhi is often explained as from the mouth of the Guru. It's the alphabet the Sikh scripture is written in, and the one Punjabi is written in across India today. Now, it's worth being careful here. Guru Angad didn't invent writing out of nothing. Scripts much like it were already used in the Punjab, especially by traders keeping accounts. What Sikh tradition credits him with is shaping those letters into a clear, standard alphabet, putting them in order, and teaching them, so anyone could learn to read the Guru's words. Tradition says he taught the letters to children himself, and helped put together an early primer. Think about what that means. On many paths, the holy words sat in a language only specialists could read, so ordinary people needed someone in between. Guru Angad did the opposite. He put the hymns in the people's own language, in letters a farmer's child could learn, so the word could go straight from the page into anyone's life. That's a big part of why, to this day, Sikhs treat reading the scripture as something for everyone, man or woman, of any caste. There's no priestly class that holds the book. Anyone who can read Gurmukhi can read the Guru. And the first symbol you learned, Ik Onkar, the numeral one and its curve, is written in these letters.
screen: `GURMUKHI — FROM THE GURU'S MOUTH.` · `SHAPED, ORDERED AND TAUGHT.` · `THE PEOPLE'S OWN LANGUAGE.` · `NO ONE STANDS BETWEEN.` · then, large: `LETTERS FOR EVERYONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: write your name slowly by hand. Find a pen and any scrap of paper. Write your name, one letter at a time, slower than you ever do. Watch each shape form. Somebody taught you these letters once. Maybe you remember who. A parent at a kitchen table, a teacher in a classroom. Let your pen move slowly enough to remember them. The bell holds the time.
Gurmukhi. The script Guru Angad shaped and taught at Khadur, from the mouth of the Guru, so ordinary people could read the hymns themselves.
Your line: letters for everyone. Today, explain one thing you know in the plainest words you can, so anyone could understand it. Day forty-five.

howItsDone: Sikh children often learn Gurmukhi at home or in gurdwara classes so they can read the Guru Granth Sahib themselves; any Sikh, of any gender or caste, may read from the scripture.

notes: Gurmukhi's origins: scholars link it to Sharada-derived Landa/Takri scripts; tradition credits Guru Angad with standardizing it. The script avoids claiming invention. Confirm phrasing.
Etymology 'from the mouth of the Guru' is the common explanation; some explain it as 'the script of the gurmukhs'. Confirm.
'An early primer' (the Bal Bodh tradition) stated loosely; confirm or cut.
Ik Onkar written in Gurmukhi letters: the symbol combines the Gurmukhi numeral and letter; confirm.
